title: The key in the commit history
brief: 17:50. A developer tells you they committed an API key by mistake, and removed it in the next commit. They say it is safe now.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: Git keeps every version of every file. The next commit hid the key, it did not remove it.
teaches: A committed secret is compromised the moment it is pushed: rotate first
Purging history is a clean up on top of rotation, never a replacement for it
Scan for secrets before they are pushed, so it is caught in seconds

value.title: Repository history review
value.intro: Look at the file as it is now, then look at its history the way anyone with a clone of the repository can.

attempts.label: Read the current config file
attempts.response:
module.exports = { apiUrl: '...', apiKey: process.env.BANK_API_KEY };

The key is not in the current file.

attempts.label: Search the full history for the key
attempts.response:
commit a1c4f08  Add bank export config
+   apiKey: 'hb_live_51Kx9dLmP0aR3vT8kW1cN6sY9fK4',

Still there, in a commit every clone of the repository contains.

attempts.label: Try the key against the bank's API

fix.prompt: Pick every step, in the order that matters most: deal with the exposed key first.

options.label: Revoke the key and issue a new one, stored in a secrets manager
code: + new key -> secrets manager, injected as BANK_API_KEY
options.why: The key was exposed the moment it was pushed. Only revoking it makes the copy in history useless.

options.label: Remove the key from history with a rewrite tool, and have everyone re-clone
code: + force-push, then ask every developer and every CI cache to re-clone
options.why: Tidies up what is left, so it stops turning up in searches. It comes after rotation, never instead of it.

options.label: Add secret scanning before push and in CI
options.why: Catches the next one in seconds, and finds any that are already in the repository.

options.label: Leave it: the next commit already removed it
options.why: The old commit is untouched. That is the whole problem.

options.label: Squash the last two commits on your machine
options.why: The commit is already on the server and in every clone. Rewriting your local copy does nothing to theirs.

options.label: Make the repository private
options.why: Everyone who already cloned it still has the key, and so does every mirror and every cache.

setup.title: Workbench
setup.body: Check whether the removed key is really gone

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.objective: Reproduce the bug: read the Code tab, then use the Exploit tab on staging.
exploit.insight: Git keeps every version of every file. The next commit hid the key, it did not remove it.

hint.text: Open the Workbench. Read the code, try normal use on the Exploit tab, then send the request that breaks it.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: The next commit stopped the key being used in the code, but the commit that added it is still there, and anyone can search for it. The key worked against the bank.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: Removed from the file, still in the repository
body: The next commit stopped the key being used in the code, but the commit that added it is still there, and anyone can search for it. The key worked against the bank.
Git is a history. Nothing in it is ever really “deleted in the next commit”.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: Revoking the key made the old one useless, which is the only thing that truly fixes it. Purging history removes the leftover, and scanning means the next mistake is caught before it leaves a developer's machine.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: Rotated first, cleaned second, scanned always
body: Revoking the key made the old one useless, which is the only thing that truly fixes it. Purging history removes the leftover, and scanning means the next mistake is caught before it leaves a developer's machine.
Rotation first. Everything else is tidying.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: Squashing on your machine, making the repository private, or hoping the next commit was enough all leave the live key in copies you cannot recall. It still opens the bank.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: The key still works
body: Squashing on your machine, making the repository private, or hoping the next commit was enough all leave the live key in copies you cannot recall. It still opens the bank.
A secret that was pushed is a secret that leaked: revoke it.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
